name: LM393 Dual Comparator
summary: Two comparators in the same DIP-8 arrangement as the LM358 op-amp, with open-collector outputs. The two look identical on a board and are not interchangeable.
notes: The outputs are open collector. Without a pull-up resistor to your logic rail, nothing comes out at all. 10k is the usual choice; lower if the line is long or fast.

Same package and same pin arrangement as the LM358, which is why they get swapped by mistake. The LM358 is an op-amp with a push-pull output and will not work as a comparator at speed; the LM393 has no frequency compensation and will oscillate if you close a feedback loop around it.

With no hysteresis a slow input makes the output chatter across the threshold. Add positive feedback from output to the non-inverting input, a few hundred k, to turn it into a Schmitt trigger. Nearly every real comparator circuit needs this.
Open collector means you can wire several outputs together on one pull-up and get a wired-AND, which is how multi-channel alarm circuits are built.
Input common mode range goes down to ground but stops about 1.5 V below V+, the same limitation as the LM358.
The LM339 is four of these in a DIP-14, at the cost of a different pinout.

circuit.title: Comparator with hysteresis

parts.why: The output is an open collector. It can only pull low, so without this there is no high level at all.
Positive feedback. A few millivolts of hysteresis stops the output chattering as the inputs cross.

circuit.note: Open collector cuts both ways: it is why you can wire several outputs together as an AND, and why a comparator with no pull-up looks dead on a scope.
